title: ICS for EMS: Command Structure
learningObjectives: Apply the ICS principles that matter on an EMS scene: unity of command, span of control, modular growth, common terminology.
Distinguish command staff from general staff and name each position.
Map the EMS/Medical Branch structure under Operations.
Perform a correct transfer of command and explain unified command.

summary.title: Why ICS
summary.content: ICS (Incident Command System, part of NIMS) gives every agency the same org chart, titles, and language, so a medic from another county can plug into your scene in seconds. It grows and shrinks with the incident (modular): a 5-patient crash may be IC + Triage only; a stadium collapse fills the whole chart. Every position not filled is held by the person above it — so the IC owns everything until delegated.

summary.title: The Principles You Actually Use
summary.content: Unity of command: everyone reports to ONE supervisor. Span of control: one supervisor manages roughly 3–7 people/units, ~5 is optimal — beyond that, add a layer. Common terminology: plain language and standard titles. Management by objectives via an Incident Action Plan (IAP; verbal for small incidents). Accountability: check-in, assignments tracked. Chain of command: orders flow down, info flows up — no freelancing.

summary.title: Command Staff vs General Staff
summary.content: COMMAND STAFF (report directly to IC, title = Officer): Safety Officer (can stop unsafe acts immediately), Public Information Officer (media), Liaison Officer (other agencies). GENERAL STAFF (title = Section Chief): Operations (does the work — EMS lives here), Planning (situation, resources, IAP, documentation), Logistics (supplies, facilities, comms equipment, food, responder medical), Finance/Admin (costs, time, claims). Memory: 'Officers advise, Chiefs execute'.

summary.title: ICS Titles by Level
summary.content: Incident Commander → Section = Chief → Branch = Director → Division (geographic) / Group (functional) = Supervisor → Unit = Leader → Strike Team / Task Force = Leader → Staging Area = Manager. Division = WHERE (Division A = front of building, Division 2 = 2nd floor). Group = WHAT (Medical Group, Rescue Group). The EMS piece is usually the Medical Group (or Medical Branch when large).

summary.title: EMS Inside ICS
summary.content: Operations Section → Medical Branch Director (large incidents) → Medical Group Supervisor → Triage Unit Leader (with triage teams; morgue manager), Treatment Unit Leader (with Red/Yellow/Green treatment managers), Patient Transportation Unit/Group Leader (with Medical Communications Coordinator and ground/air ambulance coordinators), plus Medical Supply Coordinator. Staging Area Manager reports to Operations (or IC early). Chapter 4 covers each role's action card.

summary.title: Transfer of Command & Unified Command
summary.content: Transfer of command: face-to-face whenever possible; brief situation, objectives, hazards, resources, org chart; announce the change on the radio so everyone knows who is IC now. Arriving senior officers don't automatically take over — they assume command only after a formal transfer. Unified Command: when multiple agencies share jurisdiction (fire, police, EMS, public health), their commanders co-locate at one command post and produce ONE set of objectives/IAP — each agency keeps authority over its own people.

clinicalPearls: If you're the first EMS unit, you ARE every ICS position until you hand one off.
When your span exceeds ~5, don't work harder — add a supervisor layer.
The Safety Officer can halt any unsafe act on the spot without waiting for the IC.
A freelancer — a crew acting without assignment — is a safety and accountability hazard, no matter how well-intentioned.
redFlags: Two people both believing they're IC (no formal transfer).
Units self-dispatching into the scene instead of checking in at staging.
Agencies running parallel command posts with conflicting objectives.
commonMistakes: Calling a Section 'Branch' or a Unit 'Group' — titles carry meaning.
Forgetting that unfilled positions stay with the supervisor above.
Transferring command by radio only, without a briefing.
Thinking unified command means one agency gives up its authority.
memoryAids: Command Staff = 'SLP': Safety, Liaison, PIO — they're Officers.
General Staff = 'OPLF' (Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance) — 'Only Paramedics Love Food' — they're Chiefs.
Titles ladder: Chief → Director → Supervisor → Leader → Manager (staging). 'Cheerful Directors Supervise Lazy Managers.'

decisionTrees.title: Scale the Org Chart
decisionTrees.content:
Small MCI (≤ ~10 pts)
  → IC (first EMS officer) + Triage + Transport
Medium MCI
  → IC → Medical Group Supervisor → Triage / Treatment / Transport Unit Leaders + Staging
Large / multi-agency MCI
  → Unified Command + Command Staff (Safety, PIO, Liaison)
  → Operations Section Chief → Medical Branch Director → Medical Groups / Divisions
  → Planning, Logistics, Finance as needed
Rule: span of control > ~5–7 → add a layer
